items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to resale of tickets to places of entertainment; to amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating to tickets to places of entertainment, in relation to the effectiveness thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S8340

TITLE OF BILL:

An act
to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to resale of
tickets to places of entertainment; to amend chapter 704 of the laws of
1991, amending the arts and cultural affairs law and chapter 912 of the
laws of 1920 relating to the regulation of boxing and wrestling relating
to tickets to places of entertainment,
in relation to the effectiveness thereof

PURPOSE:

This bill would amend and reinstate effective until May 15, 2011
Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law (ACAL), which sunset
on May 15, 2010, make ACAL § 25.11 permanent, and make various other
changes to the law governing ticket sales.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.03 to add a new
subdivision (10) to create the definition for a "ticket office."

Section 2 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.11 to add a new
subdivision (4) to create the definition of a "ticket office."
Section 3 of the bill would include ticket offices as locations
protected by a 1,500 foot buffer zone, inside of which tickets cannot
be resold.

Section 3 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.11 to include a ticket
office within the scope of the buffer zone provisions set forth by
this section.

Section 4 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.15 to clarify how the
Secretary of State can draw upon bonds posted by the licensees of
Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law.

Section 5 of the bill would amend chapter 704 of the laws of 1991 to
extend the effectiveness of Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural
Affairs Law.

Section 6 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.25 to require that
licensees report to the Consumer Protection Board information related
to the resale of tickets.

Section 7 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.29(1) to require that
service charges in association with tickets sold be reasonable.

Section 8 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.30 to require that
consumers be provided with the option of a transferrable ticket at
the time of first public sale.

Section 9 of the bill would amend ACAL § 25.35 to add a new
subdivision (7) to allow for increases in fines for certain
violations of ACAL Article 25 when such violations are committed by
firms, corporations or entities other than individual persons.

Section 10 of the bill would create a new ACAL § 25.24 to prohibit the
use of automated ticket purchasing software.

Section 11 of the bill would make ACAL § 25.11 permanent.

Section 12 of the bill would make the bill effective immediately.

EXISTING LAW:

The regulatory framework governing the sale and resale of tickets to
places of entertainment is contained in Article 25 of the ACAL

STATEMENT IN SUPPORT:

This legislation would reinstate ACAL Article 25, which expired on May
15, 2010 and reverted to a governance framework contained in the
formerly dormant Article 25 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law as
promulgated generally by the Laws of 1920. The purpose of this
reinstatement is to end the disruption in the ticket sale and resale
marketplace caused by the sunset, and to provide new protections to
consumer of tickets.

The bill would prohibit the use of automated ticket purchasing
software, which presently is used by unscrupulous speculators to
purchase tickets at initial sale ahead of consumers intending to
attend an event. While the use of this software is typically banned
by the policies of ticket issuers and venue operators, this statutory
prohibition would allow the State to intervene to further protect
consumers.

This legislation would also provide new consumer protections on the
primary market, by prohibiting venue operators and their agents from
employing paperless ticketing systems that do not allow consumers to
transfer their tickets independent of the operator or operator's
agent, unless the operator offers the consumer a choice of purchasing
independently transferrable tickets in another form. While the
legislation would clarify that operators or their agents may utilize
and maintain their own will-call window and other ticket exchange
services, it would affirm that these services would not constitute
independently transferrable ticketing options to satisfy the consumer
option requirements established in the legislation. Additionally,
operators would be prohibited from charging higher prices based on

the form of ticket a consumer selects, and would be allowed to assess
only reasonable surcharges on other than paperless forms of tickets.

Further, the legislation would provide for a new reporting requirement
for licensees that would enable the State to better determine the
impact of the resale marketplace on consumers, as well as to study
the purchasing trends of consumers.

The bill also would allow for operators or their agents to restrict
the resale of promotional, discounted or free tickets provided to
specific individuals or groups of individuals. This language would
acknowledge that instances whereby the operators or their agents
confers something of value in a ticket transaction to consumers
because of their status in a group or community, such as student or
civic groups, or disabled or economically disadvantaged persons,
constitute reasonable circumstances for the restriction of the resale
of such tickets, which otherwise would not have been sold to the
general public with the same benefits. However, the language would
provide that the resale of promotional tickets that are offered to
the general public can not be restricted by the operator or
operator's agent.

Finally, the bill would make permanent ACAL § 25.11, which relates to
ticket office buffer zones.

BUDGET IMPLICATIONS:

This legislation would not have any impact on the State's Financial
Plan.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act would take effect immediately, but would provide that the
provisions related to paperless ticketing would not impact paperless
tickets sold prior to the enactment of this act.
